title: Immediate excludes Church authority as faith's foundation, not the Church's teaching ministry
source_text: X. Verum quum fidei nostrae certitudinem de Scripturae divinitate immediate referendam dicimus ad internam Spiritus sancti persuasionem, instant adversarii: ea quae fidei sunt, quale est hunc et illum librum divinitus esse conscriptum, non amplius haberi per immediatas revelationes, sed juxta Dei ordinationem ab Ecclesia docente disci et accipi debere: alioqui fenestram apertum iri fanaticis et Enthusiastis. Resp. Quum dicitur aliquid immediate credi, per illuminationem et impulsum Spiritus sancti, id duobus modis intelligi posse. Primo quidem ut excludatur opera et ministerium hominum explicantium et commendantium ea quae credenda sunt; quo pacto Paulus Apostolus Evangelium non acceperat ab homine, neque per hominem, sed immediate a Spiritu sancto edoctus erat. Hujusmodi immediata Spiritus revelatio non amplius locum habet in Ecclesia Dei. Neque Spiritus sanctus, communiter et juxta viam ordinariam, sic fidelibus revelat hos et illos libros esse divinitus conscriptos. Sed fides de Scriptura nobis ingeneratur per operam et ministerium Ecclesiae tradentis et commendantis libros sacros. Verum alio sensu dici potest Scripturam immediate credi per internum Spiritus sancti testimonium; nempe, ut excludatur extranea quaevis authoritas, sive verbi cujusdam non scripti, sive docentis Ecclesiae, quae sit fidei nostrae argumentum proprie dictum, quo fidem nostram Spiritus fundare intelligatur. Atque ita Scripturae immediate credimus, quoniam ea fides quam Scripturae adhibemus, et quam Spiritus Dei nobis imprimit, non nititur proprie ullo argumento et medio externo, nec in verbo aliquo quod in ore sit Ecclesiae fundatur. Non secus ac, ex mente Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, fides illa quae praebetur Ecclesiae docenti, et proponenti Dei verbum, quod in ejus ore esse credunt, non nititur aliena quadam authoritate, quae sit a verbi illius authoritate diversa: neque etiam habet pro argumento testimonium et vocem Ecclesiae, quandoquidem idem esset sui ipsius argumentum, sed immediate est ex illuminatione et instinctu Spiritus sancti. Qui tamen etiam, ex eorum mente, utitur motivis quibusdam quibus homines ad fidem Ecclesiae adhibendam disponat; qualia sunt quae ipsi notas Ecclesiae vocant. Itaque per vocem illam immediate excludimus authoritatem Ecclesiae tanquam fidei nostrae fundamentum, non vero simpliciter Ecclesiae docentis operam et ministerium.
pass_a_gloss: But when we say that the certainty of our faith concerning Scripture's divinity is to be referred immediately to the inward persuasion of the Holy Spirit, the adversaries press: things that belong to faith, such as that this and that book was written by divine inspiration, are no longer had by immediate revelations, but by God's ordinance ought to be learned and received from the teaching Church: otherwise a window would be opened to fanatics and Enthusiasts. Reply. When something is said to be believed immediately, by the illumination and impulse of the Holy Spirit, that can be understood in two ways. First, so that the work and ministry of men explaining and recommending the things to be believed is excluded; in which way the Apostle Paul had not received the Gospel from a man, nor through a man, but had been taught immediately by the Holy Spirit. Immediate revelation of the Spirit of that kind no longer has place in the Church of God. Nor does the Holy Spirit, commonly and according to the ordinary way, thus reveal to the faithful that these and those books were written by divine inspiration. But faith concerning Scripture is generated in us through the work and ministry of the Church handing down and recommending the sacred books. Yet in another sense Scripture can be said to be believed immediately by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit; namely, so that any foreign authority is excluded, whether of some unwritten word, or of the teaching Church, which would be the properly so-called argument of our faith, by which the Spirit would be understood to found our faith. And so we believe Scripture immediately, because that faith which we give to Scripture, and which the Spirit of God impresses on us, does not properly rest on any external argument and means, nor is it founded on some word that is in the mouth of the Church. Not otherwise than, on the mind of the Doctors of the Roman Church, that faith which is given to the teaching Church, and to her proposing God's word which they believe to be in her mouth, does not rest on some alien authority different from the authority of that word: nor does it even have for its argument the testimony and voice of the Church, since that would be an argument of itself, but it is immediately from the illumination and instinct of the Holy Spirit. Who nevertheless also, on their mind, uses certain motives by which he disposes men to give faith to the Church; such as those which they themselves call the notes of the Church. Therefore by that word immediately we exclude the authority of the Church as the foundation of our faith, but not simply the work and ministry of the teaching Church.
pass_b_english: But when we say the certainty of our faith about Scripture's divinity is to be referred immediately to the Spirit's inward persuasion, the adversaries press hard: things that belong to faith — that this or that book was written by divine inspiration — are no longer had by immediate revelations, but by God's ordinance must be learned and received from the teaching Church; otherwise a window opens to fanatics and Enthusiasts.
Reply. Saying something is believed immediately by the Spirit's illumination and impulse can mean two things.

First, it can shut out the work and ministry of people who explain and commend what is to be believed — the way Paul received the Gospel not from a man nor through a man, but was taught immediately by the Holy Spirit. Immediate revelation of that kind no longer has a place in God's Church. Nor does the Spirit, in the common and ordinary way, reveal to the faithful which books were written by divine inspiration. Faith about Scripture is generated in us through the Church's work and ministry as she hands down and recommends the sacred books.

Yet in another sense Scripture can be said to be believed immediately by the Spirit's inward testimony: namely, so that any foreign authority is shut out — whether some unwritten word, or the teaching Church — that would be the properly so-called argument of our faith by which the Spirit founds that faith.

So we believe Scripture immediately because the faith we give it, and which God's Spirit impresses on us, does not properly rest on any external argument or medium, nor is it founded on a word in the Church's mouth.

Likewise, on the Roman Doctors' own view, the faith given to the teaching Church as she proposes God's word (which they believe is in her mouth) does not rest on some alien authority different from that word's authority, nor even take the Church's own testimony and voice as its argument — that would be an argument of itself — but is immediately from the Spirit's illumination and instinct. He still, they say, uses motives that dispose people to trust the Church, which they call the Church's notes.
So by immediately we exclude the Church's authority as faith's foundation, not simply the teaching Church's work and ministry.
